system.overview: The Chicago 'L' is the rapid transit system serving the city of Chicago and some of its surrounding suburbs. Operated by the CTA, it is the fourth-largest rapid transit system in the United States by ridership. The system's name comes from the elevated railways that make up much of the network, though portions also run in subway tunnels, at grade, and in highway medians.

history.title: First L Line Opens
history.description: The Chicago and South Side Rapid Transit Railroad opens the first L line, running from Congress Street to 39th Street (now Pershing Road).

history.title: Metropolitan West Side Elevated Opens
history.description: The Metropolitan West Side Elevated Railroad begins service, becoming the second L company in Chicago.

history.title: Union Loop Opens
history.description: The Union Elevated Railroad opens the Loop, the iconic downtown circuit connecting all L lines.

history.title: Northwestern Elevated Opens
history.description: The Northwestern Elevated Railroad begins service on the north side, later becoming part of the Brown and Purple lines.

history.title: State Street Subway Opens
history.description: The State Street subway opens as Chicago's first subway tunnel, carrying what would become Red Line service through downtown.

history.title: CTA Formed
history.description: The Chicago Transit Authority is created by the Illinois state legislature, unifying the city's private transit companies under public operation.

history.title: Dearborn Street Subway Opens
history.description: The Dearborn Street subway opens, carrying Blue Line service through the Loop. The Milwaukee-Dearborn-Congress corridor is completed.

history.title: Congress Expressway Line Opens
history.description: The Congress Expressway median line opens, the first rapid transit line built in a highway median in the United States.

history.title: Dan Ryan Line Opens
history.description: The Dan Ryan branch opens in the median of the Dan Ryan Expressway, extending South Side service to 95th Street.

history.title: Kennedy Expressway Line Opens
history.description: Rapid transit service begins in the Kennedy Expressway median, connecting the Northwest Side to the Loop.

history.title: O'Hare Extension Opens
history.description: The Blue Line extension to O'Hare International Airport opens, providing direct rail access to the airport.

history.title: Orange Line Opens
history.description: The Orange Line opens, connecting Midway Airport to the Loop via the Southwest Side.

history.title: Lines Receive Color Names
history.description: CTA adopts a color-based naming system for all L lines, replacing the legacy route names with Red, Blue, Green, Brown, Orange, Purple, and Yellow.

history.title: Pink Line Opens
history.description: The Pink Line begins full-time service to the 54th/Cermak branch, previously a branch of the Blue Line with limited service.

history.title: Brown Line Capacity Expansion
history.description: The $530 million Brown Line Capacity Expansion Project is completed, lengthening all 18 Brown Line stations to accommodate eight-car trains.

history.title: 5000-Series Fleet Complete
history.description: The final 5000-series railcar is delivered, completing the order of 714 cars built by Bombardier. They replace the entire 2200-series and 2400-series fleets.

history.title: Wilson Station Rebuilt
history.description: The new $280 million Wilson station opens with a transfer between the Red and Purple lines, replacing the century-old structure.

history.title: 7000-Series Enters Revenue Service
history.description: The first CRRC Sifang America-built 7000-series railcars enter revenue service on the Blue Line, beginning the replacement of the 2600-series fleet.

history.title: Red Line Extension Groundbreaking
history.description: Construction begins on the Red Line Extension, which will extend the line 5.6 miles south from 95th/Dan Ryan to 130th Street with four new stations.

red.name: Red Line
red.description: The Red Line is the busiest L line, running north-south through the city from Howard on the far North Side to 95th/Dan Ryan on the South Side. It uses the State Street subway through downtown and is the backbone of the CTA rail system.

blue.name: Blue Line
blue.description: The Blue Line is the longest L line, connecting O'Hare International Airport on the Northwest Side to Forest Park on the West Side. It uses the Dearborn Street subway through the Loop and runs in the Kennedy and Eisenhower expressway medians.

brown.name: Brown Line
brown.description: The Brown Line serves the North Side, running from Kimball in Albany Park to the Loop elevated. It is one of the most heavily used lines and underwent a major capacity expansion completed in 2012.

green.name: Green Line
green.description: The Green Line is the oldest line in the system, tracing its origins to the first L line that opened in 1892. It runs east-west on the West Side via Lake Street and splits into two branches on the South Side at Ashland/63rd and Cottage Grove.

branches.name: Ashland Branch
branches.description: Alternating trains on the South Side

branches.name: Cottage Grove Branch
branches.description: Alternating trains on the South Side

orange.name: Orange Line
orange.description: The Orange Line connects Midway International Airport to the Loop elevated, serving the Southwest Side. It was the first new L line built since the 1970s when it opened in 1993.

pink.name: Pink Line
pink.description: The Pink Line serves the near West and Southwest sides, running from 54th/Cermak to the Loop elevated. The branch formerly had limited Blue Line service before becoming the full-time Pink Line in 2006.

purple.name: Purple Line
purple.description: The Purple Line serves Evanston and Wilmette on the North Shore, running from Linden to Howard with weekday rush-hour express service to the Loop. It is one of the oldest segments of the L system.

branches.name: Loop Express
branches.description: Weekday rush-hour express service to the Loop

yellow.name: Yellow Line
yellow.description: The Yellow Line, also known as the Skokie Swift, is the shortest L line. It provides a non-stop shuttle between Dempster-Skokie in Skokie and Howard, where it connects to the Red and Purple lines.

railcars.name: 4000 Series
railcars.description: The 4000 Series were the first all-steel cars on the L system, built in multiple orders from 1914 to 1924. They came in two variants: 'Baldies' with metal roofs and six doors per car, and 'Plushies' with wooden roofs and green plush seats. They were the last CTA cars with air brakes.

railcars.name: 6000 Series
railcars.description: The 6000 Series was the largest single order in CTA history, with 720 cars built using PCC streetcar technology. They were the first L cars designed as permanently coupled married pairs and incorporated components salvaged from Chicago's retired PCC streetcar fleet.

railcars.name: 1-50 Series
railcars.description: The 1-50 Series were similar to the 6000 Series but built as double-ended single cars rather than married pairs. Some were equipped with trolley poles for overhead wire operation on the Evanston and Skokie lines. Ten cars were later converted to married-pair sets for Skokie Swift service.

railcars.name: 2000 Series
railcars.description: The 2000 Series were the first of the 'High Performance Family' of L cars. They introduced air conditioning, fluorescent lighting, large picture windows, and sculpted fiberglass front ends to the L system. Built with aluminum car bodies by Pullman-Standard.

railcars.name: 2200 Series
railcars.description: The 2200 Series were the first stainless steel L cars, featuring unpainted fluted sides. They were the last cars with the blinker door configuration, which could not accommodate wheelchairs, requiring them to be paired with 2600-series cars on ADA-compliant lines.

railcars.name: 2400 Series
railcars.description: The 2400 Series were the first L cars with sliding doors, replacing the blinker door design. Originally delivered in a red, white, and blue bicentennial color scheme. They were the last cars to operate on the Orange Line before retirement.

railcars.name: 2600 Series
railcars.description: The 2600 Series were built for the O'Hare extension of the Blue Line. With 600 cars, they are the largest active fleet on the L. Car 3200 was the final railcar ever built by the Budd Company. They are being replaced by the 7000-series.

railcars.name: 3200 Series
railcars.description: The 3200 Series introduced computer-controlled cab functions and fluted steel siding to reduce graffiti. They were built for the opening of the Orange Line in 1993. A mid-life overhaul was completed in 2018, adding LED destination signs and rebuilt propulsion systems.

railcars.name: 5000 Series
railcars.description: The 5000 Series were the first AC-motor cars on the L system. Built by Bombardier, they feature LED destination signs, security cameras, aisle-facing longitudinal seating, and interior LED information displays. They make up the entire Pink, Green, Yellow, Purple, and Red Line fleets.

railcars.name: 7000 Series
railcars.description: The 7000 Series are the newest L cars, built by CRRC Sifang America at a factory in Chicago's Hegewisch neighborhood. They feature a hybrid seating configuration mixing forward-facing and aisle-facing seats, and are configured as semi-permanently coupled married pairs. Currently assigned to the Blue Line.
